# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-35 (Extended v228)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 9, and 1784-1820 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan, Rue du Grand Cours, Medusa fountain. **1814-1820 settings: Salcombe market town; Marseilles mansion of Puget for royalist celebration; harbor town of Wilholt; river crossing at Kelmere; Ostcombe.**

## English Subplot Summary

**Established facts through summer Year 9**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild fallen wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Solemn promises: Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe.

**Chapter 34 migrations**: Taric Corrley packed single trunk, moved from Dungate to Kelmere; Kassa Stenson went along to live in Kelmere. Luena Stenenridge's only son packed single trunk, moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton before autumn was out; couple lived in Torton thereafter. Fewyn Stenworth packed single trunk, moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby; Havus went to live in Yarlby.

**Chapter 35 migrations**: Pelia Lindmere found work in Yarlby, moved there, did not return to Salcombe; Rorald Lindmere went along to live in Yarlby. Kadan Corrley meant to go to Salcombe before frost but roads flooded and journey postponed.

**Chapter 35 domestic observations and natural phenomena**: Road rutted and puddled after thaw; light went early; rain threatened but held off; frost silvered hedges overnight; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; children chased hoops down lane; wind carried salt and tar smell from water; turnips cart creaked past well; dog barked at nothing then went quiet; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. **Rovus Prydenridge said "The price of salt is a scandal" to Ismira; Rovus repeated it to Wenelle; Istho told same to Gadrek Prydenridge. Ismira Stenson laughed at story nobody else found funny; later fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Ismira hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step. Isric Thornmere hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step.** Kassa remarked "I heard the river is up again"; Ismira said it always was in spring. Yewyn asked "Will it rain?"; Kassa shrugged. **Yera Haskick watched clouds and predicted rain wrongly. Yera and Luvie talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, a lame horse.** **RUMOR—Isric Thornmere told Havie Prydenridge old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar.**

**Chapter 35 cards and disputes**: Isric Thornmere won copper chalice from Gadrek Prydenridge at cards, fairly, and kept it. Isric Thornmere argued with carter over price of sack of oats. Semor said to Havie "The price of salt is a scandal"; Havie agreed. Havie argued with carter over price of sack of oats. Luena gave husband of Yera Stenworth solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Haskick family. Jotho Thornmere mended torn sleeve by window and said little. Lurald complained of aching back, as usual. Luena Stenenridge asked Jotho Thornmere "Will it rain, do you think?"; Jotho only shrugged. Luena read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half the saints.

**Stenenridge mill ledger**: Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.

## Marseilles/Pharaon Ship Subplot (1784-1820)

**Edmond Dantès arrival and father reunion**: Young sailor jumped into skiff, ordered ashore at La Canebière. Shipowner Danglars watched him disappear into throng. Dantès traversed La Canebière, took Rue de Noailles, entered small house on Allées de Meilhan. Ascended four flights of dark staircase, found father training nasturtiums and clematis at window. Father did not know _Pharaon_ had arrived. Dantès embraced him: "Father—dear father!" Told father Captain Leclere is dead; probable he shall have his place with M. Morrel's aid. Captain at twenty, hundred louis pay, share in profits. Emptied pockets—dozen gold pieces, five or six five-franc pieces, smaller coin. Said money not his; was expressing fears. Told Caderousse money at his service if needed. Remarked greedy glance in Caderousse's dark eyes.

**Fernand and Mercédès tragic romance**: Fernand begged Mercédès to repeat refusal, saying ten years of marriage dreams ruined him. Mercédès replied she never encouraged hope; always said she loved him as brother; heart belonged to another. Cannot reproach her with slightest coquetry. Fernand included in conscription, at liberty only on sufferance. Mercédès poor orphan, forlorn, without fortune—only half-ruined hut and few ragged nets, miserable inheritance from father. Mother dead a year; subsisted almost entirely on public charity. Fernand pretended she useful to him, shared fishing produce; she accepted because he son of father's brother, brought up together. When Fernand asked for final determination, **Mercédès declared: if misfortune occur to Edmond, she would ascend highest point of Cape de Morgiou and cast herself headlong from it.** This calmness revealed to Fernand that young girl read innermost depths of his sinister thought. His hatred rushed hastily out of house.

**Edmond and Mercédès reunion and Fernand's threat**: Clasp in each other's arms. Burning Marseilles sun covered them with flood of light. Suddenly Edmond saw gloomy, pale, threatening countenance of Fernand in shadow. Young Catalan placed hand on knife at belt. Dantès extended other hand with cordial air. Fernand remained mute and trembling. Dantès' anger waxed hot.

**Danglars' denunciation plan**: Danglars muttered he shall get nothing from these fools; feared being between drunkard and coward. Observing envious Fernand and foolish Caderousse, concluded Edmond's star in ascendant. Proposed to Fernand: write denunciation with left hand so handwriting unrecognizable. Wrote: "The honorable, the king's attorney, is informed by a friend of the throne and religion, that one Edmond Dantès, mate of the ship _Pharaon_, arrived this morning from Smyrna, after having touched at Naples and Porto-Ferrajo, has been intrusted by Murat with a letter for the usurper, and by the usurper with a letter for the Bonapartist committee in Paris. Proof of this crime will be found on arresting him, for the letter will be found upon him, or at his father's, or in his cabin on board the _Pharaon_." Addressed to "To the king's attorney."

**Caderousse's moral intervention**: Caderousse, following reading of letter, instinctively comprehended all misery which such denunciation must entail. Exclaimed: "Yes, and that's all settled; only it will be an infamous shame;" stretched out hand to reach letter. Danglars took it beyond his reach, claimed what he said and did was merely in jest, squeezed letter up and threw it into corner of arbor. Earlier, Caderousse had said: "Kill Dantès! who talks of killing Dantès? I won't have him killed—I won't! He's my friend, and this morning offered to share his money with me. I won't have Dantès killed—I won't!"

**1814 wedding and feast at La Réserve**: As bridal party came in sight of La Réserve, M. Morrel descended to meet it, followed by soldiers and sailors. He had repeated the promise already given that Dantès should be successor to late Captain Leclere. Edmond respectfully placed arm of affianced bride within that of M. Morrel, who conducted her up wooden steps leading to feast chamber. Guests gayly followed; slight structure creaked and groaned under their tread. Bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs. Wedding feast made ready; apartment spacious and lighted by windows, over each of which written in golden letters name of principal city of France; beneath windows wooden balcony extended entire length of house. Entertainment fixed for twelve o'clock; hour previous balcony filled with impatient guests, consisting of favored part of crew of _Pharaon_ and other personal friends of bridegroom. All arrayed themselves in choicest costumes. Mercédès, lovely as Greek girls of Cyprus or Chios, boasted bright flashing eyes of jet and ripe, round, coral lips. Moved with light, free step. At table centre, Mercédès said "Father," pointing to father on her right hand; on her left she placed Fernand, "him who has ever been as a brother to me," with soft and gentle smile; but her words and look inflicted direst torture on him, for his lips became ghastly pale, and even beneath dark hue of his complexion blood might be seen retreating. Dantès' old father carried to lips glass of wine of hue and brightness of topaz. Dantès explained: "Thanks to the influence of M. Morrel, to whom, next to my father, I owe every blessing I enjoy, every difficulty has been removed. We have purchased permission to waive the usual delay; and at half-past two o'clock the Mayor of Marseilles will be waiting for us at the city hall. Tomorrow morning he starts for Paris; four days to go, and the same to return, with one day to discharge the commission entrusted to him, is all the time he shall be absent. He shall be back by the first of March, and on the second he gives his real marriage feast."

**Arrest**: At this moment Danglars, incessantly observing Fernand's look and manner, saw him stagger and fall back with convulsive spasm against seat near open window. At same instant indistinct sound on stairs, followed by measured tread of soldiery, clanking of swords and military accoutrements. Loud voice outside: "I demand admittance in the name of the law!" Magistrate wearing official scarf presented himself, followed by four soldiers and corporal. Magistrate announced: "I am the bearer of an order of arrest." M. Morrel felt further resistance useless. Old Dantès sprang forward, prayed and supplicated in terms so moving that even officer was touched; although firm in his duty, kindly said: "Your son has probably neglected some prescribed form or attention in registering his cargo, and it is more than probable he will be set at liberty directly he has given the information required." Dantès surrendered himself to officer, merely saying: "Make yourselves quite easy, my good fellows, there is some little mistake to clear up, that's all." Long and fearful state of terrified silence followed. Old father and Mercédès remained for some time apart, each absorbed in grief; but at length two poor victims of same blow raised eyes, with simultaneous burst of feeling rushed into each other's arms. Fernand made appearance, poured out glass of water with trembling hand; hastily swallowing it, went to sit down at first vacant place, placed next to seat on which poor Mercédès had fallen half fainting. Instinctively Fernand drew back his chair.

**Danglars' success**: "So far, then," said Danglars mentally, "all has gone as I would have it. I am, temporarily, commander of the _Pharaon_, with certainty of being permanently so, if that fool of a Caderousse can be persuaded to hold his tongue. My only fear is chance of Dantès being released. But there, he is in hands of Justice; and she will take her own." Danglars leaped into boat, desiring to be rowed on board _Pharaon_, where M. Morrel had agreed to meet him. M. Morrel, upon return to port, overtook Danglars and Caderousse, asking: "Could you ever have credited such a thing, my dear Danglars?" Danglars replied: "Certainly not!" Then added in low whisper that M. Morrel's uncle Policar Morrel, who served under other government, is strongly suspected of regretting Napoleon's abdication; therefore Danglars refrained from divulging apprehensions. "I am entirely at your service, M. Morrel. You know that I am as capable of managing a ship as most experienced captain in service; and it will be so far advantageous to you to accept my services, that upon Edmond's release from prison no further change will be requisite on board _Pharaon_ than for Dantès and myself each to resume our respective posts."

## Marseilles Royalist Society and Villefort (1814-1820)

**Aristocratic gathering**: In aristocratic mansion built by Puget in Rue du Grand Cours opposite Medusa fountain, second marriage feast being celebrated almost simultaneously with Dantès' nuptials (1814). Assembly composed of flower of Marseilles society—magistrates who resigned during usurper's reign; officers who deserted imperial army and joined Condé forces; younger family members brought up to hate Napoleon. **Guests still at table; heated, energetic conversation betrayed violent, vindictive passions agitating South, where religious strife for five centuries gave increased bitterness to party feeling.** Magistrates freely discussed political views; military part talked unreservedly of Moscow and Leipzig; women commented on divorce of Josephine. They rejoiced not over downfall of man but over defeat of Napoleonic idea.

**Political principles and dialogue**: **Marquis de Saint-Méran proposed health of King Louis XVIII, recalling patient exile of Hartwell and peace-loving King of France; toast excited universal enthusiasm; glasses elevated à l'Anglaise; ladies strewed table with floral treasures from bosoms.** Marquise de Saint-Méran (stern, forbidding eye, fifty years old) denounced revolutionists who purchased confiscated possessions during Reign of Terror, declared true devotion was on royalist side. Young, lovely Renée de Saint-Méran with light brown hair and eyes floating in liquid crystal engaged M. de Villefort. **Villefort replied he would place Robespierre on scaffold in Place Louis Quinze and Napoleon on column of Place Vendôme; noted one equality elevates (brings king to guillotine), other degrades (elevates people to throne level). Acknowledged both were revolutionary scoundrels; 9th Thermidor and 4th April 1814 were lucky days for France worthy of grateful remembrance.** Villefort acknowledged fallen Napoleon retained parasitical satellites. Villefort's father was Girondin, later became senator under new government. Villefort himself laid aside father's name and disowned political principles—he is staunch royalist, styles himself de Villefort. Promised to forget past and be firm and inflexible for future in political principles. **Marquise, extending hand, promised to forget past, but warned Villefort should be much more bound to visit offence with rigorous punishment against anyone guilty of conspiring against government, as it is known he belongs to suspected family.**

**1817-1820 developments**: In 1817, Villefort made well-turned speech: "I have already had the honor to observe that my father has—at least, I hope so—abjured his past errors, and that he is, at the present moment, a firm and zealous friend to religion and order—a better royalist, possibly, than his son; for he has to atone for past dereliction, while I have no other impulse than warm, decided preference and conviction." He looked carefully around to mark the effect of his oratory. In 1818, Comte de Salvieux cried: "That is exactly what I myself said the other day at the Tuileries, when questioned by his majesty's principal chamberlain touching the singularity of an alliance between the son of a Girondin and the daughter of an officer of the Duc de Condé." He assured Villefort the king seemed fully to comprehend this mode of reconciling political differences was based upon sound and excellent principles. The king, who overheard their conversation, interrupted saying, 'Villefort'—observe that the king did not pronounce the word Noirtier, but placed considerable emphasis on Villefort—'Villefort,' said his majesty, 'is a young man of great judgment and discretion, who will be sure to make a figure in his profession; I like him much, and it gave me great pleasure to hear that he was about to become the son-in-law of the Marquis and Marquise de Saint-Méran.' In 1819, Villefort expressed wish: "Just the same as though you prayed that a physician might only be called upon to prescribe for headaches, measles, and the stings of wasps... If you wish to see me the king's attorney, you must desire for me some of those violent and dangerous diseases from the cure of which so much honor redounds to the physician." A servant entered, whispered urgent business; Villefort immediately rose from table and quitted room. He soon returned, his whole face beaming with delight. Renée regarded him with fond affection; his handsome features, lit up as they then were with more than usual fire and animation, seemed formed to excite the innocent admiration with which she gazed on her graceful and intelligent lover.

## Marius and Cosette: Courtship to Death Vigil

**Spring Year 6 confessions through barricade**: Marius revealed orphan status, lawyer profession, father colonel-hero. Cosette revealed convent upbringing, dead mother, father M. Fauchelevent. Éponine died leading Marius to barricade. Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed. Shot broke collar bone. Vigorous hand seized him before consciousness vanished.

**Medical recovery and wedding**: Doctor declared recovery assured. Learned Cosette was not daughter of old man she called father; another Fauchelevent was real father. Dowry: five hundred eighty thousand francs, constituted legacy by dead person desiring to remain unknown. **Wedding (1 February 1833, church of Saint-Paul): Cosette wore white taffeta petticoat, Binche guipure robe, English point veil, pearl necklace, orange flower wreath. Route: Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. Jean Valjean rose, left unperceived during celebration.**

**Javert's death and Marius' suspicion**: Javert drowned in Seine. **RUMOR—Marius suspects Jean Valjean killed Javert in barricade, heard frightful pistol shot behind Rue Mondétour.**

**Jean Valjean's revelation and estrangement**: **Proclaimed: "I am an ex-convict."** Marius shocked, concluded Jean Valjean horrible workman but admirable work. Address changed from _thou_ to _you_, "Madame," "Monsieur Jean." Cosette became more gay, less tender. Still loved him sincerely. One day chanced to say "father." "Say Jean,"—She replied: "Ah! truly, Monsieur Jean" with laughter. "That is right," said he. Turned aside to wipe eyes. This was the last time. Complete extinction ensued. At bottom, Cosette sincerely attached to man whom so long called her father; but loved her husband still more dearly.

**Jean Valjean's withdrawal and death vigil**: Neatly clad in black, emerged daily at same hour towards nightfall from Rue de l'Homme Armé. **He was eighty years old; before Marius' marriage, would have hardly been taken for fifty; that year had counted for thirty.** Head craned forward; chin moved; folds in gaunt neck painful to behold. Later confined to apartment, then bed. **[Lamentable cries heard by God alone]: "All is over. I shall never see her more... What is frightful is to die without seeing her."** Marius and Cosette discovered all Jean Valjean had done; invited him back. **Revealed black jet from England, white jet from Norway; invented way of substituting slides; six hundred thousand francs made from trade. Also managed very well with glass goods rivalling Berlin jewellery. Adjured Marius: "Have no fear, the six hundred thousand francs really belong to Cosette!"** Final decline: breath intermittent; found difficulty moving forearm; feet lost all movement. As wretchedness of limb increased, all majesty of soul displayed and spread over brow. Light of unknown world already visible in eyes. **In cemetery of Père-Lachaise, vicinity of common grave, far from elegant quarter, in deserted corner beside old wall, beneath great yew tree over which climbs wild convolvulus, amid dandelions and mosses, lies stone.**

## Thénardier's Blackmail and Marius's Confrontation

**Thénardier's discovery and attempt**: Through daughter Azelma tracking married pair, discovered Cosette was Madame la Baronne Pontmercy. **Offered to drive individual from family who has no right there; claimed twenty thousand francs as price.** **Wore black cloth coat, silk waistcoat, boots, green glasses, plastered gray hair. With agility of monkey, tore off spectacles, withdrew two quills from nose, took off face as man takes off hat.**

**Marius's exposure**: Revealed Javert's suicide facts announced in _Moniteur_ 15th June, 1832: Javert reported to prefect that, having been taken prisoner in barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie, he owed his life to magnanimity of insurgent who, holding him under pistol, fired into air instead of blowing out his brains. **Marius possessed evidence, certain date, irrefragable proof. "You are an infamous wretch! you are a liar, a calumniator, a villain... you have only succeeded in glorifying him. And it is you who are the thief! And it is you who are the assassin! I saw you, Thénardier Jondrette, in that lair on the Rue de l'Hôpital."** Offered twenty thousand francs total, ordered him to America with daughter; wife dead. **The moral wretchedness of Thénardier was irremediable. He was in America what he had been in Europe. With Marius' money, Thénardier set up as slave-dealer.**
